newsitem.title: UK: Britain lambasts Afghanistan on heroin trade.
newsitem.headline: Britain lambasts Afghanistan on heroin trade.

text.p: A British minister accused Afghanistan's dominant Taleban Islamic militia on Wednesday of using funds from the international heroin trade to buy weapons.

"The Taleban acquiesce in and benefit from the opium production and in the drug trade out of Afghanistan," Derek Fatchett, a junior minister at the foreign office, wrote in the daily Guardian. "Drugs money replenishes the Taleban's war chest."
He warned that long-term aid would depend on the fight against drugs, saying 95 percent of opiates reaching Western Europe came from the "Golden Crescent" of Afghanistan and its neighbours.
"It is no exaggeration to say that the lives of our young people will be determined by our ability to stop the flow of drugs from Afghanistan," Fatchett wrote.

"That is why we will be watching events in Afghanistan, and the Taleban's actions on the drugs problem, ever more closely in the weeks and months ahead," wrote Fatchett, the minister responsible for Britain's relations with Asian countries.
The Taleban, which is backed by Pakistan, controls more than two-thirds of Afghanistan and has imposed a strict and austere version of Islam hostile to Western influence.

But its seat at international bodies is contested by most nations. The United Nations wants a broad-based government in Kabul that would represent all the country's ethnic, religious and political groups.
Fatchett said the drug problem in Britain could be partly blamed on Afghanistan's Islamic Taleban militia.

"Afghanistan is the heart of the problem. A supply-led flood of heroin originating from there is facing us on the streets of Britain," wrote Fatchett, who has just returned from a trip to India and Pakistan.
Fatchett said donors, Britain amongst them, had been "generous" with humanitarian aid for Afghanistan, devastated by Soviet intervention in the 1980s and factional fighting in its aftermath.

"But in the long term, the readiness of the international community to give the development assistance the country will need after the war will depend on Afghan cooperation in efforts to curb drugs production and trafficking," Fatchett wrote.
"Afghanistan and the Taleban are not just far-away places and people. What they do, especially on drugs, matters to us all."
